title: Learn to taste
intro: Tasting means looking, smelling and sipping with attention, always in the same order. You don't need a special palate: you need a method and some practice.

eye.lead: Look at the glass against a white background, tilting it slightly. The colour tells you the wine's age and gives clues about the grape.
how: Fill the glass up to a third.
Tilt it 45° over a sheet of white paper or a white tablecloth.
Look at the core (intensity) and at the rim (colour and age).

red: A very young wine: a purple rim is typical of its first year.
A few years old: the colour is starting to evolve.
A developed wine, with many years of ageing.
white: Oak-aged or a few years old, or a sweet wine.
Very developed, oxidative, or a sweet wine with long ageing.
rose: Some development, or made from a deeply coloured grape.

eye.tears_txt: The tears (or legs) running down the glass show alcohol and sugar: more tears, more alcohol or sweetness. They say nothing about quality.

keys.t: Whether the wine is clear or hazy. A hazy wine may have a fault, or may be deliberately unfiltered.
How it reflects light. Young wines with good acidity tend to look brighter.
How dark the colour is at the core of the glass: pale, medium or deep.
The hue itself: purple, ruby, garnet or tawny in reds; lemon, gold or amber in whites.
The edge of the wine when you tilt the glass. It's where age shows best.
The drops running down the side of the glass. They indicate alcohol and sugar, not quality.

nose.lead: The nose is the richest part of tasting: much of what we call "flavour" we actually perceive through smell.
how: First nose: smell it with the glass still. The most volatile aromas show up.
Swirl the glass in circles on the table: the wine takes in oxygen and opens up.
Second nose: smell it again, with short sniffs.
nose.still_txt: With the glass still, only a few soft aromas come through.
nose.swirl_txt: When you swirl, the wine is aerated and the aromas multiply.

layers.d: They come from the grape and from fermentation.
They come from winemaking: oak, yeast, malolactic conversion.
They appear with years in bottle or with long ageing.

faults.t: Smells of wet cardboard or a damp cellar. The fruit disappears.
Smells of bruised apple or walnut, and the colour is browner than expected.
Smells of rotten eggs or a struck match. Sometimes it goes away when the wine is aerated.
Smells of vinegar or nail varnish when excessive.

keys.t: Whether the wine is clean (sound) or faulty.
How easily you can pick up the aromas: light, medium or pronounced.
Smelling with the glass still and then after swirling.
Whether the wine smells youthful (fresh fruit), developing or fully developed (tertiary aromas).
How many different aromas appear and how they change in the glass.

mouth.lead: Take a small sip, move it all around your mouth and, if you like, draw in a little air: that way the aromas reach the back of your nose (retronasal).
how: Attack: the first impression as the wine enters.
Mid-palate: how it develops in the middle of the mouth.
Finish: what remains after swallowing or spitting, and how long it lasts.
mouth.myth: The "tongue map" (sweet on the tip, bitter at the back) is a myth: every part of the tongue perceives every taste. It comes from a misreading of a 1901 paper.
mouth.comp_t: Move each slider and it tells you what you'll feel

comps.feel: You feel it as soon as the wine enters, on the tip of the tongue and throughout the mouth. Most still wines are dry.
It makes your mouth water. Notice how much saliva builds up after swallowing: more saliva, more acidity.
It dries and roughens your gums and tongue, like very strong tea. Almost only in reds.
It gives a warming sensation in the throat and chest after swallowing.
The weight of the wine in your mouth: like the difference between water, skimmed milk and whole milk.
How long the flavours last after swallowing. Use the timer.

mouth.timer_res: {s} seconds. The longer the finish, the more complex and higher quality the wine tends to be.

keys.t: The first sensation as the wine enters your mouth.
Aromas that reach the nose from the mouth. That's why tasters draw in a little air.
The wine's "backbone": acidity, tannin, alcohol and body.
When no component sticks out: not the acidity, the alcohol or the tannin.
How long the flavour lasts after swallowing. Also called the finish.

end.lead: To assess quality, tasters use four questions (BLIC). Tick the ones that apply to the wine you're tasting.

blic.t: Are the fruit, acidity, tannin and alcohol in harmony?
Does the finish last long enough?
Do the aromas and flavours come through clearly?
Do many different aromas appear, changing in the glass?

levels_txt: It does well on two of the four.
ready: Drink now: not suitable for ageing
Can drink now, but has potential for ageing
Too young: best kept for later

game.d: We pour you a mystery wine. Look at it, smell it and taste it, fill in the sheet and guess what it is.
game.q_aromas: Swirl the glass and tick the aromas you recognise
game.q_mouth: Taste it: how does it feel?

tannin: It dries your gums a little.
It dries your gums quite a lot.
It roughens and dries a lot, like very strong tea.
acid: It barely makes your mouth water.
It makes your mouth water a little.
It makes your mouth water quite a lot.
body: It fills your mouth, like whole milk.

sheet.d: Fill it in while you taste a real wine. It's saved in this browser and you can print it or save it as a PDF.

sources: Sources: WSET, "Systematic Approach to Tasting Wine" (SAT), Level 3 (2022); Chandrashekar et al., Nature 444 (2006), on taste receptors (tongue map myth).
